slides.heading: Validate Subsequence
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Easy · Arrays
slides.narration: Let's solve Validate Subsequence, an easy arrays problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Is `sequence` obtainable from `array` by deleting elements without reordering?
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Is sequence obtainable from array by deleting elements without reordering?

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: A subsequence keeps order, so we just try to match the sequence's elements one by one while scanning the array.
slides.narration: A subsequence keeps order, so we just try to match the sequence's elements one by one while scanning the array.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Brute force: try every way to pick positions → exponential
Optimal: one greedy pass, matching in order
Greedy is safe: matching early never hurts
slides.narration: A brute-force approach would try every way of choosing positions in the array, which is exponential. But matching each sequence element at its earliest opportunity is always safe, so one pass with two indices is enough.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Keep an index into the sequence
3. Advance the index on every match
4. Valid if the index reaches the end
slides.narration: Step by step. First, keep an index into the sequence. Second, scan the array. Third, advance the index on every match. Fourth, valid if the index reaches the end.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 1 matches → advance j to 1
slides.narration: The array value 1 matches the next sequence item, so j advances to 1.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 6 matches → advance j to 2
slides.narration: The array value 6 matches the next sequence item, so j advances to 2.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: -1 matches → advance j to 3
slides.narration: The array value -1 matches the next sequence item, so j advances to 3.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 10 matches → advance j to 4
slides.narration: The array value 10 matches the next sequence item, so j advances to 4.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: j = 4 = len(sequence) → valid
slides.narration: We matched every element of the sequence, so it's a valid subsequence.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We keep an index into the sequence. Scanning the array, whenever the current value equals the next sequence element, we advance that index. The answer is whether the index reached the sequence length.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n. Space is constant.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Repeated values: each array element used once
slides.narration: If the sequence is longer than the array it can't be a subsequence. Each array element can only be used once, which the single forward pass guarantees.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Follow-up: check many sequences against one array
slides.narration: Clarify the difference between a subsequence and a subarray: subsequences don't have to be contiguous. A follow-up is checking many sequences quickly, where you'd preprocess positions of each value.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: A subsequence keeps order, so we just try to match the sequence's elements one by one while scanning the array.
slides.narration: To recap Validate Subsequence: A subsequence keeps order, so we just try to match the sequence's elements one by one while scanning the array. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
